diagrams.title: Psoriasis Treatment by Extent, Impact, and Phenotype
diagrams.subtitle: BSA alone underestimates special-site disease and psoriatic arthritis

foundation.text: Emollient + site-appropriate topical corticosteroid; vitamin-D analogue or fixed combination; calcineurin inhibitor/roflumilast for sensitive sites; adherence and maintenance plan.
foundation.detail: Severity is not BSA alone. Confirm diagnosis, triggers, treatment technique, and patient goals; use proactive intermittent maintenance for recurrent sites.

conventional.text: Usually unnecessary unless topical burden, access, or patient preference makes phototherapy more practical.

advanced.text: Usually unnecessary, but low BSA does not preclude escalation when special-site disease or quality-of-life burden is high.

foundation.text: Optimize formulations for scalp, face/folds, genital, palmoplantar and nail disease; assess pain, function, sexual health, sleep and work impact.

conventional.text: NB-UVB or targeted phototherapy for suitable skin disease; apremilast, deucravacitinib, methotrexate, cyclosporine or acitretin selected by phenotype and comorbidity.

advanced.text: Reasonable when topical burden is unsustainable, special-site disease is refractory, PsA is present, or quality-of-life impairment is substantial despite low BSA.

foundation.text: Continue topicals for residual lesions and difficult sites; screen PsA and cardiometabolic/psychosocial comorbidity.

conventional.text: NB-UVB, methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin, apremilast or deucravacitinib according to desired speed, monitoring, pregnancy potential, liver/renal risk and joint disease.

advanced.text: Choose a biologic by skin efficacy, PsA domains, IBD/uveitis, pregnancy planning, infection history, dosing preference, prior response and access—not by a universal hierarchy.

rows.name: Erythrodermic, generalized pustular or acutely unstable disease

foundation.text: Hospitalize when systemic instability, fluid/electrolyte disturbance, infection concern, or extensive painful disease is present; stop provoking drugs and avoid abrupt systemic-steroid withdrawal.

conventional.text: Rapid systemic control may include cyclosporine, infliximab or other phenotype-specific therapy; generalized pustular psoriasis has distinct IL-36–directed options.

advanced.text: Select urgent therapy with dermatology/inpatient expertise; exclude AGEP, infection and other erythroderma/pustular mimics before committing to long-term strategy.

foundation.text: Emollients and limited site-appropriate topical corticosteroids; avoid topical retinoids. Coordinate obstetric care for extensive disease.

conventional.text: NB-UVB is preferred when phototherapy is needed. Methotrexate and acitretin are contraindicated; other systemic choices require individualized review.

advanced.text: Certolizumab has minimal placental transfer and the strongest pharmacokinetic rationale among biologics; decisions for all agents remain disease- and trimester-specific.

citations.quote: AAD-NPF guideline reviews biologic treatment selection and monitoring in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis.
GRAPPA recommends domain-based PsA treatment that accounts for skin, joints, axial disease, enthesitis, dactylitis, associated conditions, and comorbidities.
EULAR 2023 PsA update links pharmacologic escalation to active domains, treatment targets, and extra-musculoskeletal manifestations.

diagrams.title: Psoriatic Arthritis Treatment by Active Domain
diagrams.subtitle: Peripheral, axial, entheseal, skin, bowel, and ocular domains can require different mechanisms

initial.text: NSAID for short-term symptoms when appropriate; early csDMARD (often methotrexate) can be used for active peripheral polyarthritis, especially with skin disease.

targeted.text: TNF, IL-17, IL-23, JAK or other targeted therapy after inadequate response or when prognostic severity warrants earlier escalation.

selection.text: Skin severity, IBD/uveitis, infection, cardiovascular/VTE risk, pregnancy and prior biologic response determine mechanism.

initial.text: Exercise/physical therapy and NSAID when appropriate; confirm inflammatory axial disease rather than mechanical pain.

targeted.text: TNF inhibitor, IL-17 inhibitor or selected JAK inhibitor. IL-23/IL-12/23 mechanisms are not preferred for clinically active axial disease.

selection.text: Recurrent uveitis favors monoclonal TNF; active IBD generally favors monoclonal TNF or an IBD-effective mechanism and argues against IL-17.

initial.text: Local measures and NSAID/injection in selected cases; avoid injecting directly into high-risk tendons.

targeted.text: TNF, IL-17, IL-23, JAK or PDE-4–pathway therapy according to severity and co-domains.

selection.text: Objective inflammation and functional impact matter; central sensitization can coexist and should not drive unnecessary escalation.

initial.text: Topicals and phototherapy remain adjuncts; nail disease requires long response assessment and can signal PsA risk.

targeted.text: IL-17 and IL-23 agents generally offer high skin efficacy; TNF and ustekinumab remain effective. Use an agent that also treats the dominant musculoskeletal domain.

selection.text: Special-site burden, speed, dosing interval, IBD and candidiasis risk refine choice.

initial.text: Coordinate gastroenterology and document bowel activity before changing therapy.

targeted.text: Use an agent effective for both PsA and the specific IBD phenotype—monoclonal TNF, ustekinumab, selected IL-23 or JAK agents are examples.

selection.text: Generally avoid IL-17 in active IBD; do not assume every member of a class has the same bowel indication.

initial.text: Ophthalmology co-management; topical ocular therapy alone may be inadequate for recurrent posterior disease.

targeted.text: Monoclonal TNF inhibition is generally preferred when uveitis is a major domain.

selection.text: Etanercept is not preferred for uveitis; choose based on ocular phenotype and prior response.
